name: Phrenology head and psychograph

card.summary: A china phrenology bust and a 1900s-30s head-measuring machine that mapped skull shape to supposed character traits, used as a novelty self-assessment of face and head.
card.note: A historical novelty; phrenology is regarded as a discredited pseudoscience.

quick.overview:
The phrenology head is a china bust marked with zones for supposed mental faculties; the psychograph was a machine that measured a head at 32 points and printed a character rating. Both come from phrenology, the idea that skull shape reveals personality.

In appearance culture they are historical curiosities and a reference point for modern head and face shape reading.
quick.how: Phrenologists felt and measured the skull and consulted charts and busts. The psychograph, patented by Henry Lavery, was placed in theatre lobbies and department stores as a novelty.
quick.risks: Phrenology is regarded as pseudoscience; modern imaging studies contradict its claims. The machines carry no known physical risk.

lead: The phrenology head is a ceramic bust that maps mental faculties onto zones of the skull, made famous by Lorenzo Fowler.[2] The psychograph was a phrenology machine invented by Henry C. Lavery, first patented in 1905, which measured the head at 32 points and rated faculties on a five-point scale from deficient to very superior.[1]

Phrenology originated with Franz Joseph Gall, who began lecturing in 1796, and was spread by Johann Spurzheim and George Combe.[2] It drew criticism early and lost scientific credibility by the 1840s; modern imaging has contradicted its central claims.[2]
The Psychograph Company (1929-1937) placed machines in theatre lobbies and department stores, and the device kept public interest in phrenology alive into the 1930s before sales fell.[1]

chain: Head measured or read by bust chart
angle.text: The objects offered a way to read character from head contours; they are now collected as curiosities.

paras: Phrenologists ran hands over skulls and used charts naming faculties; Gall listed 27 organs and later phrenologists expanded the number.[2] Fowler china heads became a lasting symbol of the movement.[2]

Lavery lived in Superior, Wisconsin when he patented the first version, later partnering with Frank P. White to form the Psychograph Company.[1] A unit is displayed at the Museum of Questionable Medical Devices at the Science Museum of Minnesota.[1]
No studies found. Phrenology was challenged by Flourens ablation experiments and Broca findings, and modern imaging has disproved its central claims.[2]
